The move prompted the Maoists' largest coalition partner to quit the government, the party's leader said. Under the deal, more than 19,000 former insurgents were to be integrated into the country's security forces. But two weeks ago, the government asked Katawal to explain why he went to the Supreme Court to challenge the government's refusal to extend the tenure of eight brigadier generals in March. Government spokesman Krishna Bahadur Mahara said Sunday that the government was not satisfied with Katawal's explanation and fired him -- three months before his scheduled retirement -- in a meeting that the Maoists' coalition partners boycotted. Pokharel said his party urged the Maoists not to fire Katawal without a consensus in the country's parliament. He said the Maoists, led by Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, ignored that advice. The Maoists could continue to hold power with the support of smaller parties, but Pokharel said his party is working to form a new ruling coalition. The Cabinet named an interim army chief, but presidential spokesman Rajendra Dahal told CNN that 18 parties in Nepal's parliament asked Yadav to keep Katawal on the job. There was no immediate reaction from the government on the president's decision.

The decision led the Maoists’ biggest coalition ally to withdraw from the government, the party’s leader said.

“Without consensus, the ongoing peace process will not reach its logical conclusion and the drafting of the new constitution will not be possible,” said Ishwor Pokharel, general secretary of the Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist). “The consensus that existed so far has come to standstill.”

Backers of both camps in the dispute went into the streets on Sunday to protest. Although the rival groups clashed at times, no major injuries were reported.

The Maoists gave up their weapons and came to power in the 2008 elections following a deal that brought an end to a 10-year insurgency. According to that agreement, more than 19,000 former fighters were supposed to be incorporated into Nepal’s security forces.

Two weeks earlier, the government had demanded that Katawal justify his decision to petition the Supreme Court over the government’s refusal in March to prolong the terms of eight brigadier generals.

Government spokesman Krishna Bahadur Mahara said Sunday that Katawal’s response did not satisfy the government, leading to his dismissal three months before his planned retirement. The decision was made at a meeting boycotted by the Maoists’ coalition partners.

Pokharel said his party had called on the Maoists not to remove Katawal unless there was agreement in Nepal’s parliament. He said the Maoists, headed by Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, disregarded that recommendation.

“We do not like the way the Maoists’ way of functioning,” Pokharel said.

The Maoists control 238 seats in the 601-member parliament, while Pokharel’s party holds 109. Although the Maoists could remain in power with backing from smaller parties, Pokharel said his party is attempting to put together a new governing alliance.

The Cabinet appointed an acting army chief, but presidential spokesman Rajendra Dahal told CNN that 18 parties represented in Nepal’s parliament had asked Yadav to allow Katawal to remain in his post.

The government did not immediately respond to the president’s decision.

**Nepal crisis deepens after Maoist-led government fires army chief**

*KATHMANDU, Nepal —* Nepal’s fragile peace process was thrown into fresh uncertainty after the Maoist-led government moved to dismiss the country’s army chief, triggering a confrontation with the president, the collapse of key coalition support and protests in the streets of the capital.

Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, better known by his nom de guerre Prachanda, ordered the removal of Gen. Rookmangud Katawal after accusing him of defying civilian authority. The dispute centered on Katawal’s resistance to government directives, including issues tied to recruitment, retirement of senior officers and the integration of former Maoist fighters into the national army — one of the most sensitive provisions of Nepal’s peace agreement.

But President Ram Baran Yadav rejected the dismissal, instructing Katawal to remain in his post and setting up a constitutional standoff between the president and the elected government.

The decision has exposed deep divisions in Nepal’s postwar political order. The Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist), a major coalition partner, withdrew support from the government, saying the Maoists had acted unilaterally. The move left the Maoist-led administration politically weakened and raised questions over whether it could continue to govern.

Opposition parties and critics accused the Maoists of trying to politicize the army and consolidate control over state institutions. Maoist leaders countered that the army chief had repeatedly challenged an elected civilian government and that his removal was necessary to uphold democratic authority over the military.

Tensions spilled into the streets, with rival demonstrations in Kathmandu and other areas. Maoist supporters denounced the president’s intervention as unconstitutional, while opposition groups rallied against what they described as an attempt by the former rebels to dominate the army.

At the heart of the crisis is Nepal’s unfinished transition from a decade-long civil war that killed more than 13,000 people and ended with a 2006 peace deal. The agreement brought the Maoists into mainstream politics, led to the abolition of the monarchy and established Nepal as a republic. But the integration and rehabilitation of thousands of former Maoist combatants has remained a major sticking point.

The national army has long resisted large-scale incorporation of ex-rebel fighters, while the Maoists have argued that integration is a core commitment of the peace process. The confrontation over Katawal has intensified fears that mistrust between the former insurgents, the army and other political parties could derail progress toward a new constitution and lasting stability.

Analysts say the president’s move may have prevented an immediate shake-up of the military leadership, but it also created a potentially dangerous precedent by placing the presidency and the cabinet on opposing sides of a dispute over command authority.

The crisis now leaves Nepal facing multiple uncertainties: whether the Maoists can hold together a government, whether opposition parties can form an alternative coalition, and whether the peace process can survive a direct clash over the role of the army.

For many Nepalis, the dispute is more than a power struggle between politicians and generals. It is a test of whether the country’s new republican institutions can manage conflict through constitutional means — and whether the promises made at the end of the civil war can still be fulfilled.

**Nepal plunges into political crisis after army chief refuses dismissal**

**KATHMANDU, Nepal —** Nepal’s fragile coalition government was thrown into crisis after the Maoist-led administration ordered the dismissal of the country’s army chief, only for the general to refuse to step down and the president to intervene in his favor.

The confrontation deepened further when the Communist Party of Nepal-Unified Marxist Leninist, or UML, a key coalition partner, announced it was withdrawing from Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal’s government. The move left the Maoist-led administration politically weakened and raised fears of renewed instability in the Himalayan republic, which is still emerging from a decade-long civil war.

The dispute centers on Gen. Rookmangud Katawal, Nepal’s chief of army staff, whom the government accused of defying civilian authority. The cabinet decided to remove him after a series of disagreements between the Maoist leadership and the army, including disputes over recruitment, the extension of senior officers’ terms and the integration of former Maoist combatants into the national army — a central provision of the peace process that ended the insurgency in 2006.

Katawal rejected the dismissal order, maintaining that the decision was improper. Shortly afterward, President Ram Baran Yadav wrote to the army chief instructing him to remain in his post, effectively countermanding the cabinet’s order and setting up a constitutional showdown between the president and the elected government.

Maoist leaders denounced the president’s intervention as unconstitutional, arguing that executive authority rests with the cabinet. Opposition parties and the army’s supporters, however, accused the Maoists of trying to politicize the military and consolidate control over state institutions.

The UML’s decision to quit the coalition deprived the Maoists of a crucial ally. Party leaders said they could not support the dismissal of the army chief without broader political consensus, especially given the sensitivity of civil-military relations in a country where the army remained largely outside Maoist control during the war.

The crisis marks one of the most serious tests of Nepal’s young republic since the abolition of the monarchy in 2008. Dahal, widely known by his wartime name Prachanda, became prime minister after the Maoists won the largest number of seats in elections for a Constituent Assembly tasked with drafting a new constitution.

But tensions have persisted between the former rebels, traditional political parties and the Nepal Army. The Maoists have long argued that thousands of their former fighters should be integrated into the army under the peace agreement. Military leaders have resisted large-scale integration, saying recruitment should be based on professional standards rather than political affiliation.

Analysts said the confrontation could derail the peace process if not resolved through negotiation. The army remains one of Nepal’s most powerful institutions, while the Maoists still command loyalty among former guerrillas living in United Nations-monitored cantonments.

“This is a direct clash over who controls the army and how far Nepal’s democratic institutions have matured,” said one Kathmandu-based political observer. “If the parties do not compromise, the entire transition could be put at risk.”

International governments and diplomats have urged restraint, calling on all sides to respect constitutional procedures and preserve the peace process. Nepal’s neighbors, India and China, are also watching developments closely. India, which has deep political and security ties with Nepal, has traditionally maintained close relations with the Nepal Army and has expressed concern over instability in Kathmandu.

For ordinary Nepalis, the standoff has revived memories of the country’s turbulent recent past: royal rule, civil war, mass protests and the difficult transition to republican democracy. The removal of the monarchy was expected to usher in a new era of elected governance, but the latest confrontation underscores how unresolved questions over power-sharing and security-sector reform continue to haunt the country.

With the UML out of the coalition, the Maoist government faced an uncertain future. Without enough support in parliament, Dahal could be forced to resign or seek a new political arrangement. Opposition parties have called for a national consensus government, while Maoist leaders have vowed to challenge the president’s move.

The immediate fate of Katawal remained a flashpoint. His continued presence at army headquarters, backed by the president’s order, signaled that the military would not accept the cabinet’s dismissal without a broader political settlement.

The crisis leaves Nepal at a pivotal moment: either political leaders find a compromise that preserves civilian rule and the peace process, or the country risks sliding back into confrontation between former enemies whose war officially ended but whose struggle over the state remains unresolved.

**Kathmandu —** Nepal’s Maoist-led Cabinet moved to dismiss the country’s army chief, Gen. Rookmangud Katawal, after months of escalating confrontation over civilian control of the military and the unresolved fate of thousands of former Maoist guerrillas promised a place in the postwar security structure under the 2006 peace agreement.

The decision, taken by Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal — better known by his wartime name, Prachanda — and his ministers, marked the sharpest civil-military crisis since Nepal’s decade-long insurgency ended and the monarchy was abolished. It also quickly turned into a broader constitutional showdown when President Ram Baran Yadav intervened to keep Katawal in his post, prompting the Maoists to accuse the president and rival parties of undermining an elected government.

At the heart of the dispute was the unfinished business of Nepal’s peace process.

The 2006 Comprehensive Peace Agreement ended a Maoist insurgency that had killed more than 13,000 people and brought the former rebels into mainstream politics. A central provision of that settlement was that the Maoists’ People’s Liberation Army would be confined to United Nations-monitored cantonments, while the Nepal Army would remain in barracks. The two sides also agreed that Maoist combatants would eventually be “integrated and rehabilitated,” with a special committee to determine how many would enter the national security forces and how others would be resettled.

But nearly three years later, the question remained explosive. The Maoists, who won the largest share of seats in the 2008 Constituent Assembly election and led the government, argued that integration was a core promise of the peace accord and essential to transforming the old royal army into a democratic national force. Many in the Nepal Army, supported by opposition parties and some coalition partners, feared that large-scale integration of Maoist fighters would politicize the military and allow the former rebels to dominate the state by other means.

General Katawal became the symbol of that resistance.

The Maoist-led government accused him of repeatedly defying civilian authority. Among the charges cited were the army’s recruitment of new soldiers despite government instructions not to do so while Maoist combatants remained in cantonments; his refusal to accept the retirement of several senior generals whose terms the government did not want extended; and the army’s decision to pull out of a national sports event after Maoist former fighters were allowed to participate. Maoist leaders said these actions showed that Katawal did not recognize the authority of the elected Cabinet and was obstructing the peace process.

Katawal and his supporters rejected that interpretation. They argued that the army was protecting its institutional integrity and resisting an attempt by the Maoists to capture the military. Opposition parties said the prime minister was less interested in civilian supremacy than in replacing an uncooperative army chief with someone more amenable to Maoist demands.

The controversy split the governing coalition. Several parties, including the Communist Party of Nepal-Unified Marxist Leninist, objected to Katawal’s dismissal, saying the move had not been agreed upon through consensus. The issue therefore became not only a dispute between the Maoists and the army, but also a test of whether Nepal’s fragile postwar institutions could resolve power struggles through constitutional procedures.

The Cabinet’s decision to sack Katawal triggered an immediate counter-move by President Yadav, who instructed the general to remain in office. The president’s intervention was welcomed by opposition parties but denounced by the Maoists as unconstitutional. They argued that Nepal’s interim constitution made the army answerable to the elected government, not to a largely ceremonial president acting independently.

The political consequences were swift and severe. Prachanda resigned as prime minister, saying he would not remain in office after what he described as a violation of civilian supremacy. The Maoists withdrew from government, bringing down the coalition and pushing Nepal into a new phase of instability. Rival parties then moved to form a new government without the Maoists, even though the Maoists remained the largest party in the Constituent Assembly.

The crisis deepened mistrust among the main forces that had jointly ended the monarchy. It also slowed the drafting of Nepal’s new constitution and complicated the integration and rehabilitation of Maoist combatants — the very issue the peace agreement had left for political negotiation.

For many Nepalis, the Katawal affair exposed the unresolved contradictions of the postwar transition: a former rebel movement trying to lead the state, an army still shaped by its royal-era hierarchy, a president testing the limits of a new republican office, and political parties unable to agree on how to merge wartime enemies into a single democratic order.

What began as the firing of one general therefore became a defining confrontation over who controlled Nepal’s army, how the 2006 peace deal would be implemented, and whether the country’s fragile republic could keep its peace process on track.
